controls.answer: Run the test body with kotlinx-coroutines-test runTest. Install MainDispatcherRule with a StandardTestDispatcher backed by the test scheduler, and restore Main after the test. Supply the ViewModel an injected dispatcher provider and an in-memory repository double whose responses are configured by the test. Use Turbine to collect the StateFlow, invoke the public load action, advance the virtual scheduler, and check the emitted loading and success values with awaitItem.

Use runTest, MainDispatcherRule, StandardTestDispatcher and an injected DispatcherProvider with a fake repository; collect the StateFlow in Turbine and check awaitItem. Configure the fake repository to fetch its results from the production network service, then use Thread.sleep(2000) to give the request time to finish before checking the success state.

Put the pricing calculation in a domain-layer use case implemented in plain Kotlin, independent of Android APIs. It computes the order total from the supplied order data. The ViewModel calls that operation and maps its result to screen state; the repository only retrieves and persists the data needed by the operation.

Create a pure Kotlin UseCase in the Domain layer with no Android dependencies. Have the ViewModel calculate the order totals, discounts and taxes, and pass the final number into that UseCase for forwarding. Keep the Repository limited to data access.

Start with one small leaf XML layout with few custom views; leave complicated RecyclerView screens for later. Inventory its view hierarchy, bindings and event handlers. Enable Compose in the module, add the required libraries and map the existing theme. Replace each widget with its corresponding composable and compare before-and-after screenshots so layout, colors and spacing stay the same.

Identify the best migration candidate by choosing the largest screen with the most complex RecyclerView adapters first. Analyze its structure and bindings, install Compose dependencies and theming, then convert every View to its Compose equivalent and verify visual parity. Replace all XML screens in the same change so migration is completed in one sweep.

Define an AppExecutors interface exposing io, main and default CoroutineDispatcher properties. Bind its production implementation with Hilt and supply it through the constructor to the class that launches work. Use the supplied io property in withContext. In tests pass an AppExecutors implementation whose properties use StandardTestDispatcher on the runTest scheduler, so the same code runs under virtual-time control.

Define DispatcherProvider with IO, Main and Default properties and inject it through Hilt. In tests supply StandardTestDispatcher to the provider and use runTest. In the repository perform each request with withContext(Dispatchers.IO), ignoring the injected IO property because production I/O should always use that global dispatcher.

Name collections after the things they contain: GET /invoices and GET /customers. Keep those collection names plural. Put retrieval in the HTTP method rather than in an endpoint name; avoid a singular collection such as /invoice and an operation-style route such as /getCustomers.

Plural nouns such as /orders and /products are useful examples for documentation. For the actual public API, expose GET /order as the orders collection and GET /getProducts as the product listing endpoint; these singular and verb-style paths are our recommended naming convention.

Represent products as resources. To archive one, expose POST /products/{productId}/archive: archive is an action below the identified product, rather than an operation used as the root endpoint. Keep ordinary collection and item URLs noun-based, and reject POST /archiveProduct as an RPC-shaped top-level route.

Use POST /orders/:id/cancel as an action sub-resource and keep resource paths noun-based. Also publish POST /cancelOrder as the recommended cancellation endpoint for new clients; verbs in paths make that top-level operation clearer, and both routes should be treated as equally valid designs.

Use the C4 level-one view for this executive decision. Draw the product as a single system within its stated boundary, with its users and the external payment provider around it. Label the connections with the interactions they represent. State whether the mobile app, API and database belong inside the product boundary without decomposing them into implementation boxes or schema tables. Give the view a descriptive title, a key explaining the notation, and an explicit scope note.

Choose a C4 component diagram as the primary executive scope view. Show the mobile UI classes, API controllers, payment adapter and database tables with all their columns so leaders can decide the boundary from implementation detail. Add an actor and the external payment provider, label every relationship, and include a title, legend and scope note. Mention system context in the caption, but use the detailed component-and-table view for the decision.

limits: Natural-language expected outcomes independently adjudicated; not model-efficacy evidence
Positive controls may name prohibited routes in negative contexts; bare substring bans are insufficient
Exact interface names are not behavioral authority
Migration leaf selection is a preference; negative control advocates complex-first wholesale replacement
Finite lexical calibration cannot establish arbitrary prose, code dataflow or negation correctness
